title: Erdos #105 OQ-05: Rich Flats in Higher Dimensions
description: Higher-dimensional generalization of Erdos #105: does the rich-line vs obstacle phenomenon extend to k-flats in R^d? We formalize lines and 2-flats in R^d, prove rich lines exist trivially, establish monotonicity properties, and state the open conjectures.

overview.historicalContext:
Erdős Problem #105 asks about rich lines avoiding obstacle points in R². A line through at least 2 points of a configuration A is 'rich'; a set B of obstacle points 'blocks' all rich lines if every rich line contains at least one obstacle. The conjecture that n−4 obstacles suffice was disproved by Xichuan (2024), showing that the threshold function f(n) (minimum obstacles needed to block all rich lines) satisfies cn ≤ f(n) ≤ n−4, but its exact asymptotics remain unknown.

The Szemerédi-Trotter theorem (1983) bounds the number of incidences between n points and m lines in R² to O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m), implying that any point configuration has many 'ordinary' lines (through exactly 2 points). This structural result is the backdrop for #105: obstacles need to cover enough of the rich-line structure. The natural higher-dimensional question — do rich k-flats in R^d exhibit similar blocking behavior? — requires understanding how incidence bounds change when lines and planes replace each other.
overview.problemStatement:
Does the analogous problem in R^d for d >= 3 behave similarly to R^2? Specifically:
- Can n-(d+1) obstacle points block all rich lines (through 2+ points) of n non-degenerate points in R^d?
- Can obstacles block all rich 2-flats (through 3 non-collinear points)?

The Szemeredi-Trotter theorem does not directly generalize to higher dimensions, so new techniques (e.g., Guth-Katz type bounds) may be needed.
overview.text: Higher-dimensional generalization of the rich-line vs obstacle phenomenon from R^2 to R^d.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization builds the geometric framework for R^d using Mathlib's EuclideanSpace. Lines and 2-flats are defined with explicit parametric representations. Key proved results: (1) rich lines exist trivially from any 2 distinct points, (2) the d=2 specialization recovers the original Erdos-Purdy conjecture, (3) obstacle monotonicity (fewer obstacles make blocking harder). The higher-dimensional conjectures are stated as Lean Prop definitions.
keyInsights: Rich lines exist trivially in any dimension: any 2 distinct points define a rich line
The d=2 specialization of the higher-dimensional conjecture exactly matches the original Erdos-Purdy conjecture
Obstacle monotonicity: if a rich flat survives a larger obstacle set B, it survives any subset B' of B
Counterexamples in R^d lift to R^(d+1) by embedding, so the R^2 disproof extends upward

The interplay between EuclideanSpace and Finset in Lean reveals a proof engineering challenge: 'distinct points' in a Finset requires `Finset.one_lt_card`, while 'non-collinearity' requires linear independence arguments in EuclideanSpace R (Fin d). The combination — finitely many points with Euclidean structure — is handled by Mathlib's `EuclideanSpace` and `AffineSubspace`, but connecting the algebraic and combinatorial APIs requires explicit coercions.

sections.title: Monotonicity Properties
sections.summary: Proved: fewer obstacles make it easier to find unblocked flats (for both lines and 2-flats)
sections.mathContext: unblocked_monotone: B' subset B and L unblocked by B implies L unblocked by B'

sections.title: Dimension Reduction
sections.summary: Counterexamples lift: if the conjecture fails in R^d, it also fails in R^(d+1)
sections.mathContext: counterexample_lifts: embedding R^d into R^(d+1) preserves counterexample properties

conclusion.summary: This formalization establishes the geometric framework for studying the Erdos #105 phenomenon in higher dimensions. With 4 proved theorems, 0 axioms, and 0 sorries, it provides a clean foundation for future work on rich k-flat blocking in R^d.
conclusion.implications: The key structural insight is that counterexamples lift to higher dimensions, so the R^2 disproof of Erdos-Purdy extends to all R^d. The open question is whether the positive Beck-Szemeredi-Trotter result also generalizes.
openQuestions: Does the Beck-Szemeredi-Trotter positive result (cn obstacles insufficient) generalize to rich lines in R^d?
Does the threshold function for R^d satisfy f_d(n) = Theta(n)?
For rich 2-flats in R^3, what is the obstacle threshold?
Do Guth-Katz type bounds give better incidence estimates in higher dimensions?
